strengths: The paper introduces two relevant and underexplored capabilities for mobile agents: proactive task suggestion and personalized task execution. The longitudinal framing is more realistic than treating every interaction as an isolated task.

FingerTip 20K is substantial in scale, containing 21,437 episodes, 506 apps, 95 users, screenshots, accessibility trees, actions, intents, and contextual metadata collected over approximately one month per user.

The evaluation covers several general-purpose multimodal models, specialized GUI agents, prompt-based agents, human performance, fine-tuning, contextual-input ablations, and limited unseen-user/app/intent experiments.
The paper is generally clear and well organized, and it acknowledges geographic limitations and some important privacy and re-identification risks.
weaknesses: The proactive-suggestion task has an inadequately validated objective. There can be many reasonable suggestions in a given context, but evaluation treats one subsequently observed intent as the answer. Exact/string similarity and an unvalidated DeepSeek-V3 binary judge may penalize useful alternatives, while the 30.3% human result itself suggests substantial ambiguity. Acceptance, utility, calibration, top-k coverage, and the cost of unwanted suggestions are not evaluated.

Crucial non-neural baselines are missing. Per-user/time-slot frequency, most-recent intent, nearest-neighbor retrieval, app-conditioned retrieval, and simple calendar/contextual predictors are necessary because the split retains the same users and repeated habits across training and test data. Without these baselines, the fine-tuning gains could reflect memorization or retrieval of recurring user-task patterns rather than the claimed proactive reasoning.

The personalization metric Sim2 is poorly justified. Levenshtein similarity between serialized action sequences is sensitive to task, app, UI state, coordinates, sequence length, and formatting rather than solely to user preference. Dividing by similarity to one trace from a different age group does not control these confounders, and computing personalization over largely unsuccessful executions can reward copying a reference trajectory even when it is inappropriate for the current state.

The supporting validation of personalization is weak. Figure 5 uses intent-nearest traces without controlling for app, device, or UI differences and provides no uncertainty or significance tests. The user study reports only four aggregate model-level pairs, no correlation coefficient, confidence interval, annotator agreement, or protocol for repeated judgments; four ordered averages are insufficient to establish metric validity.

Execution evaluation is small and insufficiently reproducible: only 200 dynamic physical-phone episodes are used, manual success checking lacks annotator counts, blinding, and agreement, and no confidence intervals or repeated trials are reported. Several reported differences correspond to only a few episodes. Procedures for resetting app/account state and handling UI or content changes are also unclear.

The unseen-user analysis contains only three users, while the main time-based split includes all users on both sides. The unseen-app and unseen-intent subsets are similarly small. These experiments do not convincingly establish generalization, particularly given possible correlations among users, apps, tasks, and interfaces.

The fine-tuned execution model reaches only 15.5% task success, far below UI-TARS at 38.5%, so the claim of effective personalized execution depends mainly on the questionable Sim2 metric. There is also no comparison against fine-tuning a strong GUI-specialized model or against generic GUI training matched for data volume.

The data-release plan raises serious unresolved privacy concerns. Longitudinal screenshots and accessibility trees are linked to timestamps, locations, demographic profiles, device information, and persistent user IDs. Participants were merely asked to avoid private information, while automated screening examines only the first and last screenshots, potentially missing sensitive intermediate screens or XML text. The paper acknowledges re-identification risk but still proposes releasing the traces without a concrete redaction, controlled-access, withdrawal, retention, or privacy-audit protocol, and no institutional ethics approval is stated.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and underexplored problem: mobile agents that infer likely user needs and adapt execution to individual behavior. FingerTip 20K is potentially valuable in scale and richness, comprising 21,437 longitudinal real-device episodes from 95 users, 506 apps, screenshots, accessibility trees, action traces, user profiles, and contextual metadata.

The evaluation covers several contemporary general-purpose and GUI-specialized models, and the appendix adds contextual ablations, limited out-of-domain tests, a human comparison, and an initial subjective assessment of the personalization metric.
The temporal split is more appropriate than a purely random episode split, and the paper openly acknowledges geographic limitations and privacy risks.
weaknesses: The central personalization construct is not convincingly established. Action-sequence differences may arise from different tasks, apps, device models, UI versions, account states, or efficiency—not stable user preferences. The preliminary analysis controls these factors inadequately, reports only six displayed intent categories, and provides no uncertainty estimates or significance tests.

Sim2 has serious construct-validity problems. It divides similarity to the target user's exact trace by similarity to a different-age user's trace selected through approximate intent matching. The denominator can reflect task and UI mismatch rather than personalization and may be unstable. Details of action serialization and similarity computation are insufficient. Validation consists of only four model-level aggregate points, with no participant-level correlation, confidence intervals, agreement analysis, or controls for task success; this does not validate the metric.

The proactive task is intrinsically underdetermined, particularly in the headline zero-screenshot setting. A 30.3% human success rate indicates substantial ambiguity rather than merely model weakness. Success is judged by DeepSeek-V3, but the paper does not validate this judge against multiple human raters or report agreement and uncertainty.

Critical simple baselines are absent: per-user most-frequent intent, time-conditioned frequency, nearest-neighbor retrieval over historical intents, population priors, and replay or retrieval of historical action trajectories. Without these, the fine-tuning gains do not demonstrate sophisticated use of context rather than memorization of repeated habits from the same users.

The principal split retains the same users and largely overlapping app and intent domains across training and testing. Fine-tuning therefore benefits from direct exposure to each person's history. The small post-hoc unseen subsets—only 3 users, 7 apps, or 4 intent categories—are too limited to substantiate broad generalization, and no confidence intervals are reported.

The personalized-execution evaluation is difficult to reproduce and insufficiently specified. It uses changing third-party apps on a physical phone, yet omits device/account initialization, app versions, state-reset procedures, evaluator blinding, annotation criteria, repeated trials, and inter-annotator agreement. Manual success judgments on only 200 episodes amplify these concerns.

Several empirical conclusions exceed the evidence. Claims of 'significant' improvement are made without statistical testing; small differences are interpreted despite missing uncertainty; and the fine-tuned model's execution success remains far below UI-TARS, while the claimed personalization advantage depends on the questionable Sim2 metric.

Privacy safeguards are not adequate for releasing longitudinal traces from personal phones. Screening only the first and last screenshots can miss sensitive information in intermediate screenshots, accessibility XML, typed text, contacts, notifications, and action contents. The dataset also links traces to profiles containing attributes such as address, occupation, age, and marital status. The paper does not clearly document institutional ethics approval, withdrawal after release, retention policy, access controls, systematic inspection of every recorded state, or concrete re-identification testing.

The cohort is small, entirely from mainland China, relatively young on average, and dominated by Chinese apps. This sharply limits claims about general mobile-agent behavior. Collection reminders, payment, training, and instructions to avoid redundant actions also weaken the assertion that the traces straightforwardly represent natural daily usage.

Reproducibility details for fine-tuning are incomplete, including optimization schedule, learning rate, epochs, model-selection procedure, seeds, and compute. Overall, the dataset idea is promising, but unresolved metric validity, missing elementary baselines, weak statistical support, reproducibility limitations, and substantial privacy concerns prevent acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored problem: moving mobile GUI agents from instruction following toward proactive assistance and user-specific behavior. The two proposed tracks are clearly motivated and meaningfully extend standard mobile-agent evaluation.

FingerTip 20K is a substantial longitudinal resource, containing 21,437 real-device episodes from 95 users across 506 apps, with screenshots, accessibility trees, actions, intents, temporal and location context, profiles, and user histories. Collecting interactions during month-long everyday use is a notable contribution over isolated simulator demonstrations.

The evaluation covers diverse general-purpose and GUI-specialized models, including strong recent baselines. The physical-device execution experiments, fine-tuning study, task-difficulty analysis, contextual ablations, cross-track experiments, and limited unseen-user/app/intent evaluations provide useful initial evidence.

Fine-tuning yields large improvements over the base Qwen-2.5-VL-7B model, and performance generally scales with training-set size and LoRA rank. These results support the central claim that longitudinal user-oriented data is useful for proactive suggestion and behavioral adaptation.

The paper discusses geographic limitations, privacy risks, consent, compensation, data filtering, and broader impacts. It also provides prompts, split statistics, and the data format, improving transparency.
weaknesses: The personalization metric is not fully convincing. Sim2 is a ratio of Levenshtein similarities between string-encoded action traces, so it can be sensitive to coordinates, sequence length, UI layout, and a potentially small denominator. Comparing against users from a different age group does not isolate individual preference from task, app, device, or demographic effects. The reported user study establishes only model-level rank agreement for four systems and provides no instance-level correlation, uncertainty, or inter-rater analysis.

The strongest personalized fine-tuned model succeeds on only 15.5% of execution tasks, substantially below UI-TARS at 38.5%. A high Sim2 on mostly unsuccessful trajectories is difficult to interpret as practically useful personalization, particularly because the paper does not clearly report personalization metrics conditioned on successful completion.

Proactive suggestion evaluation relies on DeepSeek-V3 as the binary success judge without a reported validation against human judgments. Sim1 averages embedding cosine similarity with character-level Levenshtein similarity, an insufficiently justified combination for semantically equivalent Chinese intents. Confidence intervals and statistical significance tests are absent throughout.

The main temporal split contains the same users, apps, and recurring behaviors across training and testing. This is appropriate for warm-start personalization but may allow memorization of habitual tasks and does not establish broader generalization. The unseen evaluations are small—only three held-out users, seven apps, and four intent categories—and appear to be constructed post hoc from subsets of the original test data.

The evidence that action differences represent preferences is limited: the analysis uses nearest-intent traces and coarse age-based groups, lacks controls for app/task/device differences, and reports no significance testing. The same-versus-similar-history ablation is conducted only for UI-TARS rather than the fine-tuned model underlying the strongest personalization claims.

Reproducibility remains challenging because execution uses dynamic third-party apps on physical phones and manual success judgments. Important fine-tuning and evaluation details such as learning rate, epochs, batch size, device/app-state initialization, annotator agreement, and repeated-run protocol are not reported.

The participant population is geographically and demographically narrow, with an average age of 25.9 and all contributors located in mainland China. Self-triggered, compensated collection may also differ from unprompted natural usage, limiting the generality of conclusions about everyday behavior.

The intended release presents substantial privacy risk: longitudinal screenshots, accessibility trees, timestamps, locations, and profiles can enable re-identification. Consent and filtering are positive measures, but inspecting only selected screenshots with an automated model is not a strong guarantee for intermediate frames or structured accessibility data. A clearer redaction process, release tiers, access controls, and privacy audit should precede unrestricted release.
